procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the High Court dated 08.01.2021, which dismissed Criminal Revision No. 95 of 2013 filed by the appellants.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants preferred Criminal Revision No. 95 of 2013 against the Sessions Judge's order dated 28.02.2013. The High Court dismissed this revision petition as per the impugned order dated 08.01.2021.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants, aggrieved by the High Court's order, approached the Supreme Court by filing Criminal Appeal No. 4451 of 2024. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's decision and the Sessions Judge's decision, and restored the order of the learned CJM dated 12.07.2012, effectively rejecting the complaint dated 20.07.2011 as not maintainable.

directions: Set aside the decision of the High Court dated 08.01.2021 and the decision of the learned Sessions Judge that got confirmance by the judgment of the High Court.
Restore the order of the learned CJM dated 12.07.2012.
The complaint dated 20.07.2011 stands rejected for not being maintainable.

issue.issue_text: Whether a second complaint is maintainable when the earlier one was dismissed not on its merits, but for a technical reason such as the failure of the complainant to pay process fees.

law.fact: The Supreme Court established that the maintainability of a second complaint depends entirely on how the first complaint was dismissed.
law.text_reference: maintainability or otherwise of the second complaint would depend upon how the earlier complaint happened to be rejected/dismissed at the first instance.

law.fact: The Court referenced a precedent, Jatinder Singh v. Ranjit Kaur, which held that if a complaint is dismissed for a non-merit reason, such as the complainant's default, there is no bar to filing a second complaint on the same facts.
law.text_reference: If the dismissal of the complaint was not on merit but on default of the complainant to be present there is no bar in the complainant moving the Magistrate again with a second complaint on the same facts.

law.fact: Conversely, the Court affirmed that a second complaint is not maintainable if the earlier one was disposed of on its merits after a full consideration of the case.
law.text_reference: However, second complaint would not be maintainable wherein the earlier complaint has been disposed of on full consideration of the case of the complainant on merit.

application.fact: The Court applied these principles to the specific issue of a dismissal for a technical reason, such as the failure to pay process fees.
application.text_reference: In the instant case, the question is narrowed down further as to whether such a second complaint would be maintainable when the earlier one had not been dismissed on merits, but for the failure of the complainant to put in the process fees for effecting service.

application.fact: While acknowledging the precedent that allows a second complaint after a non-merit dismissal, the Court cautioned against applying this as a universal rule.
application.text_reference: Merely because some of the decisions of this Court had held that when a Magistrate... dismissed a complaint on merits, a second complaint on the same facts would not be maintainable... it cannot be said that in all cases where a complaint... was dismissed not at the stage of Section 203, Cr.P.C., a second complaint or a second protest petition would be maintainable.

application.fact: The Court's final decision in the case from which the text is excerpted was that the second complaint was not maintainable. This was because the first dismissal, which involved the acceptance of a Final Report and consideration of a protest petition, was deemed to be a dismissal on the merits, not a purely technical one.
application.text_reference: Held: Not maintainable... If the earlier disposal of the complaint was on merits and in a manner known to law, the second complaint on ‘almost identical facts’... would not be maintainable... the CJM dismissed the first complaint vide order dated 06.06.2011 after accepting the Final Report, hearing the second respondent and considering the protest petition...

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the maintainability of a second complaint hinges on the nature of the first dismissal. While acknowledging the general principle that a dismissal for a technical reason (like failure to pay process fees) does not bar a second complaint, the Court ultimately held that this is not an absolute rule. It distinguished such technical dismissals from dismissals on the merits. In the specific case referenced, the Court found the first dismissal was on the merits, not for a purely technical reason, and therefore rejected the maintainability of the second complaint.

issue.issue_text: Whether a fresh complaint on the same set of facts is maintainable after the acceptance of a Final Report under Section 173, Cr.P.C.

facts: An initial complaint was filed, which was investigated by the police.
The police submitted a negative Final Report under Section 173, Cr.P.C., indicating no case was made out.
The complainant filed a written objection or protest petition against this Final Report.
After considering the protest petition and hearing the complainant, the court accepted the police's Final Report.
Subsequently, the complainant filed a second, fresh complaint based on the same set of facts.
law: There is no absolute or blanket bar on filing a second complaint on the same set of facts after a first one has been dismissed.
A second complaint is maintainable only under "exceptional circumstances."

Exceptional circumstances include cases where the previous order was passed on an incomplete record, there was a misunderstanding of the complaint, the order was manifestly absurd or unjust, or new facts have been discovered which could not have been brought on record earlier.
A second complaint is not maintainable if the earlier complaint was disposed of on its merits after a full consideration of the case.
application: The Court determined that when a Magistrate accepts a negative Final Report after duly considering a protest petition filed by the complainant, it constitutes a judicial order made after a full consideration of the case on its merits.
This process is not a superficial or administrative act; it involves a judicial application of mind to the facts and the investigation report.

The Court held that allowing a second complaint on the same facts without any new or exceptional circumstances would essentially permit the reopening of a case that has already been judicially decided and has attained finality.

The principle that a second complaint is barred after a decision on merits is not limited to dismissals under Section 203 Cr.P.C. but also applies to situations like this, where the substance of the complaint has been considered and rejected via the acceptance of a Final Report post-protest.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that a fresh complaint on the same set of facts is not maintainable after a court has accepted a negative Final Report, especially after considering the complainant's protest petition. This is because such a decision amounts to a disposal of the complaint on its merits, and a second complaint can only be entertained in rare and exceptional circumstances, which were not present in this case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a second complaint is maintainable when the earlier one was dismissed not on its merits, but for a technical reason such as the failure of the complainant to pay process fees.
appellant_arguments: The appellants contended that a second complaint is not maintainable, founding their argument on Section 300(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.), which pertains to the principle of double jeopardy (a person once convicted or acquitted not to be tried for the same offence).
respondent_arguments: The respondents likely argued that a dismissal for a technical reason, such as the failure to pay process fees, is not a dismissal on merits and does not amount to an acquittal. Therefore, the bar under Section 300(1) Cr.P.C. does not apply, and a second complaint is maintainable.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a fresh complaint on the same set of facts is maintainable after the acceptance of a Final Report under Section 173, Cr.P.C.
appellant_arguments: The appellants contended that a second complaint on the same facts is not maintainable after the acceptance of a Final Report. They relied on the decision in Poonam Chand Jain & Anr. v. Farzu to support this argument.
respondent_arguments: The respondents argued that a fresh complaint is maintainable. They relied on decisions such as Shivshankar Singh v. State of Bihar & Anr. and H. S. Bains v. State (Union Territory of Chandigarh), which establish that a Magistrate is not precluded from entertaining a private complaint even after accepting a final report from the police.

cases.case_name: Samta Naidu & Anr. v. State of Madhya Pradesh & Anr.
cases.principle: An order can be overturned if it was manifestly absurd, unjust or foolish.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The law does not prohibit the filing or entertaining of a second complaint, even on the same facts, provided the earlier complaint has been decided.
obiter: A court may interfere with an order if it is manifestly absurd, unjust, or foolish.
A court has the power to direct further investigation to be made by the police.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A second criminal complaint on the same facts is not maintainable, as allowing it would be contrary to the interests of justice. Once a decision has been rendered on a complaint after full consideration, the complainant cannot be given another opportunity to have the matter enquired into again, especially when it serves as an instrument of needless harassment and an abuse of the judicial process.
legal_tests_applied: The principle from Pramatha Nath that the interest of justice cannot permit that after a decision has been given on a complaint upon full consideration of the case, the complainant should be given another opportunity to have the complaint enquired into again.
The rule that a complainant is not permitted to place some evidence before the Magistrate, and then if the complaint is dismissed, adduce some more evidence in a subsequent complaint.
why_appellant_lost: The respondent's position, which was accepted by the lower courts but rejected by the Supreme Court, failed because it overlooked the fundamental principle that a complainant cannot be allowed to re-litigate a matter that has already been closed. The Supreme Court found that allowing a fresh prosecution in this context constituted an abuse of the judicial process and an instrument of harassment, which cannot be permitted.
why_respondent_won: The appellant's position, that the second complaint was not maintainable, succeeded because the Supreme Court agreed that the matter had already been closed at the instance of the respondent himself. The Court held that there can be no justification to launch a criminal prosecution afresh on the same basis, as it is the court's duty to prevent the continuation of an unnecessary judicial process and protect individuals from being subjected to prosecution on a wholly untenable complaint.
policy_considerations: The inherent power of the court must be used in the larger interest of administration of justice and for preventing manifest injustice being done.
It is a judicial obligation on the court to undo a wrong in the course of administration of justice and to prevent the continuation of unnecessary judicial process.
It is necessary to curb the menace of criminal prosecution as an instrument of operation of needless harassment.
A person cannot be permitted to unleash vendetta to harass any person needlessly.
It is the paramount duty of the court to protect an apparently innocent person from being subjected to prosecution on the basis of a wholly untenable complaint.
The whole idea of the court's inherent power (Ex debito justitiae) is to do real, complete and substantial justice for which the courts exist.
